angle: one year of her life (her age + the exact year)
title: I Was 20 in 1964. Here's What America Was Really Like

scenes.text: Sweetheart, sit here by me. You asked me what year I would go back to, if I could go back to just one. Well, I've thought about it. It's nineteen sixty-four. I was twenty years old. I'd been married for six months. And the whole country felt like it was waking up from a bad dream and dancing at the same time.
scenes.caption: IF I COULD GO BACK

scenes.text: You have to understand how that year began. Two months before, in November of sixty-three, President Kennedy was shot in Dallas. I was at the Woolworth's counter when the radio said it, and every person in that store stopped and cried. Grown men. The whole country was in mourning that Christmas. Nobody felt like celebrating anything.
scenes.caption: NOVEMBER 1963

scenes.text: Your grandfather and I lived in a little apartment over a hardware store on North Main Street in Mansfield. Two rooms and a kitchen the size of a closet. The rent was seventy-five dollars a month, and that felt like a fortune. The radiator banged all night, and the man downstairs sold paint, so the whole place smelled like turpentine. I thought it was a palace.
scenes.caption: SEVENTY-FIVE DOLLARS A MONTH

scenes.text: Your grandfather worked at the Westinghouse plant, like my father, on the line that made electric ranges. He made about two dollars and forty cents an hour. I worked at the bank downtown as a teller, until I was expecting, because in those days, sweetheart, a lot of places let you go when you started to show. Nobody thought that was strange. It was just the rule.
scenes.caption: TWO FORTY AN HOUR

scenes.text: We had one car, a nineteen fifty-seven Ford that your grandfather bought used for four hundred dollars. Gas was about thirty cents a gallon. On Sunday afternoons we'd fill it up for three dollars and just drive, out past the farms to Malabar Farm and back, with the windows down and the radio on. That was a date. It didn't cost anything.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY DRIVES

scenes.text: And then came the ninth of February. A Sunday. I will never forget it. The Beatles were on The Ed Sullivan Show. We didn't have a television yet, so we went to my parents' house on Elm Street. My brother Danny was sixteen, and he had combed his hair down over his forehead for the occasion. My father thought he looked like a sheepdog.
scenes.caption: FEBRUARY 9, 1964

scenes.text: Seventy-three million people watched that night, honey. Almost half the country. When those four boys started playing I Want to Hold Your Hand, the girls in the studio audience screamed so loud you could barely hear the music. Danny was jumping up and down on the couch. And my father, who never said anything, put down his paper and said, well, they can sing. I'll give them that.
scenes.caption: 73 MILLION

scenes.text: By April the Beatles had the top five songs in the whole country at the same time. Nobody had ever done that before. Every radio station played them every hour. Your grandfather pretended he didn't like them. Then I caught him singing She Loves You in the shower. Yeah, yeah, yeah. He never lived it down.
scenes.caption: THE TOP FIVE

scenes.text: Now let me tell you what things cost, because you won't believe me. A loaf of bread was twenty-one cents. A gallon of milk was about a dollar. A first-class stamp was five cents. A movie ticket was a dollar. A brand new house in a nice part of town was about eighteen thousand dollars. And the minimum wage was a dollar twenty-five an hour.
scenes.caption: TWENTY-ONE CENTS

scenes.text: In April Ford came out with a new car called the Mustang. It was so pretty it stopped traffic. The base price was two thousand three hundred and sixty-eight dollars. They sold twenty-two thousand of them on the very first day. Your grandfather stood in front of the dealership window on Park Avenue for twenty minutes like a little boy looking at a bicycle. We couldn't afford it. We couldn't afford it for ten years.
scenes.caption: THE MUSTANG

scenes.text: We did our shopping at the A and P on Saturday, and I had a budget of fifteen dollars a week for food. Fifteen dollars. That bought meat for every night, a roast on Sunday, eggs, butter, coffee, and a box of Jell-O for dessert. And I clipped every coupon in the Mansfield News Journal, and I saved S and H Green Stamps in little books, to trade for a toaster.
scenes.caption: GREEN STAMPS

scenes.text: And at the bank, sweetheart, I saw something every day that would make you angry. A woman could come to my window and deposit her own paycheck. But if she wanted a loan, or a charge account at the department store, she needed her husband to sign. Even if she earned more than he did. Even a widow had trouble. That didn't change until nineteen seventy-four. I'd stamp her papers and keep my mouth shut. Everybody did.
scenes.caption: HER HUSBAND HAD TO SIGN

scenes.text: That summer the World's Fair opened in New York. Everybody wanted to go. It had a giant steel globe, twelve stories high, called the Unisphere, and pavilions from all over the world, and things nobody had ever seen. A telephone where you could see the other person's face. A computer, a real one, the size of a room, that could answer questions.
scenes.caption: THE WORLD'S FAIR

scenes.text: We drove there in August, your grandfather and me, in that old Ford. It took two days. We slept in the car one night outside Harrisburg. At the General Motors pavilion they had a ride called Futurama that showed you the world of tomorrow, with cities under the ocean and on the moon. We stood in line for two hours. I thought, by the time I'm old, we'll all be living on the moon. Well. Here I am, sweetheart. Still in Ohio.
scenes.caption: THE WORLD OF TOMORROW

scenes.text: And Disney had made a boat ride for the Pepsi pavilion, with hundreds of little dolls from every country singing the same song. It's a Small World. I cried on it. I don't know why. I was twenty years old and I'd never seen anything but Ohio, and here were children from the whole world, singing together. It just got me.
scenes.query: 1964 World's Fair It's a Small World pavilion
scenes.caption: IT'S A SMALL WORLD

scenes.text: But it wasn't all music and fairs, honey. That summer, on the second of July, President Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act. It made it against the law to keep people out of a restaurant or a hotel or a job because of the color of their skin. You'd be amazed how many people in our town were angry about that. Some of them sat in my own family's church.
scenes.caption: THE CIVIL RIGHTS ACT

scenes.text: And three young men who went to Mississippi that summer to help Black families register to vote disappeared. They were found in August, buried in a dam. Two of them were from New York, one from Mississippi. I remember your grandfather reading that in the paper at breakfast and putting it down and not eating his eggs. He said, that's somebody's son. Three somebodies.
scenes.caption: FREEDOM SUMMER

scenes.text: And there was a place on the other side of the world called Vietnam, that most of us couldn't find on a map. In August the president said our ships had been attacked in a place called the Gulf of Tonkin, and Congress gave him the power to fight. It was a little story on page four. Nobody on Elm Street thought much about it. Danny was sixteen. He was going to be a mechanic.
scenes.caption: PAGE FOUR

scenes.text: Every Saturday morning I had my hair done at the beauty parlor on Park Avenue, a dollar fifty for a wash and set. The beehive was the style that year, piled up high with a whole can of Aqua Net. You slept on a satin pillow and you didn't touch it for a week. And Danny, honey, Danny spent every dollar he had on a nineteen fifty-two Chevy that didn't run. He spent the whole summer under it, in my father's driveway, singing Beach Boys songs. Little Deuce Coupe. Over and over.
scenes.caption: A WHOLE CAN OF AQUA NET

scenes.text: In the evenings we listened to the radio, because we still didn't have a TV of our own. Your grandfather would read the sports page and I'd sew. I made almost all my own clothes. A Simplicity pattern cost thirty-five cents, and a yard of cotton was about fifty cents. I made a blue dress that summer that I wore to every wedding for five years.
scenes.caption: A SIMPLICITY PATTERN

scenes.text: On Sundays we went to dinner at my mother's. Pot roast, mashed potatoes, green beans from the garden and a pie. Every single Sunday. My father carved, my mother served, and Danny ate like a horse. There was a new empty chair at that table that year. My grandmother, Pearl, had passed away the October before. Nobody sat in her chair. Not for a long time.
scenes.caption: THE EMPTY CHAIR

scenes.text: And in September, sweetheart, I found out I was expecting. Your Aunt Susan. I told your grandfather in the car, in the parking lot of the A and P, because I couldn't wait until we got home. He was so happy he drove into the shopping cart corral. We had to pay for two carts. He didn't care.
scenes.caption: THE SHOPPING CARTS

scenes.text: That fall was the election. Johnson against Senator Goldwater from Arizona. The commercials were frightening. There was one with a little girl picking petals off a daisy, and then a countdown, and an atomic bomb. They only showed it once, but everybody talked about it for weeks. Johnson won by a landslide. Forty-four states.
scenes.caption: THE DAISY

scenes.text: And the Surgeon General had said in January that cigarettes caused cancer. It was on the front page of every newspaper. And you know what? Everybody kept smoking. Your grandfather smoked Pall Malls until nineteen seventy-five. In nineteen sixty-four, honey, you could still smoke in the hospital waiting room while your wife had a baby.
scenes.caption: THE SURGEON GENERAL

scenes.text: Christmas that year, your grandfather surprised me. He'd been working double shifts in secret for two months. On Christmas morning there was a television in the corner of our little apartment, a Zenith, black and white, nineteen inches. Two hundred dollars. Bonanza on Sunday nights. I think I cried more over that television than I did at our wedding.
scenes.caption: THE ZENITH

scenes.text: So that was nineteen sixty-four, sweetheart. It wasn't perfect. Nothing ever is. There was a war starting that would break my family's heart, and there were people fighting for rights they should have had all along. But we didn't know what was coming. We were young, we were in love, and the Beatles were on the radio.
scenes.caption: WE DIDN'T KNOW

scenes.text: What I miss most is how little we needed. Two rooms, one car, fifteen dollars a week for food, and a radio. And we thought we were rich. Because we had each other, and Sunday dinner, and a whole future out there that looked like the World's Fair. That feeling. That's what I'd go back for.
scenes.caption: HOW LITTLE WE NEEDED

scenes.text: Now, what year would you go back to, if you could? And if your grandparents were young in sixty-four, ask them where they were the night the Beatles came on. Tell me in the comments. And come back tomorrow, sweetheart. Grandma has a lot more stories. Goodnight.
scenes.caption: GOODNIGHT, SWEETHEART
